title: Two-Variable Data, Part 2: Medium and Hard Problems

beats.say: In part one, we used a line of best fit to make a prediction, and we interpreted its slope. Linear data changes by a constant difference.
In this video, we decide between a linear and an exponential model, and then compute a residual for a data point.
Medium example. A table shows x equals zero, one, two, three, and y equals five, fifteen, forty-five, one hundred thirty-five. Is the data linear or exponential, and what's the model?
Check both the differences and the ratios between consecutive y values. A constant difference means linear, and a constant ratio means exponential.
Divide each y value by the one before it. The first ratio is fifteen divided by five.
Fifteen divided by five is three. The differences aren't constant, because fifteen minus five is ten, but forty-five minus fifteen is thirty.
The second ratio is forty-five divided by fifteen, the next y value divided by the one before it.
Forty-five divided by fifteen is three. The first two ratios are both three, so the pattern looks exponential.
The third ratio is one hundred thirty-five divided by forty-five, again the next y value over the previous one.
One hundred thirty-five divided by forty-five is three. Every ratio is three, so each step multiplies y by three.
The starting value, when x is zero, is five, and the factor per step is three. So the model is y equals five times three to the x.
Check with x equal to three. Three cubed is twenty-seven, and five times twenty-seven is one hundred thirty-five, which matches the table.
Hard example. A line of best fit passes through the points four comma eighteen, and ten comma thirty-three. One data point is sixteen comma forty-four point five. What's the residual for this point?
Our plan has four steps. Find the slope, find the intercept, predict y at x equals sixteen, and subtract the prediction from the actual value.
The slope is the change in y over the change in x. Both subtractions use the second point first, so the order matches.
Thirty-three minus eighteen is fifteen, and ten minus four is six. So the slope is fifteen over six.
Fifteen divided by six is two point five. So the line rises two and a half units for each one unit of x.
The line has the form y equals two point five x plus b. We substitute the first point, four comma eighteen, to find b.
Two point five times four is ten. So the equation becomes eighteen equals ten plus b.
Subtract ten from both sides. So b equals eight, and the line is y equals two point five x plus eight.
Now predict y at x equals sixteen, the x value of our data point, by substituting it into the line.
Two point five times sixteen is forty. So the prediction is forty plus eight.
Forty plus eight is forty-eight. So the line predicts forty-eight at x equals sixteen.
A residual is the actual value minus the predicted value. The actual value is forty-four point five, and the predicted value is forty-eight.
Forty-four point five minus forty-eight is negative three point five. The negative sign means the point lies below the line.
Here are the three points and the line of best fit. The line passes through the first two points exactly.
The third point, at x equals sixteen, lies a little below the line. The gray segment shows the residual, which is three and a half units long.
To recap. A constant difference means a linear model, and a constant ratio means an exponential model.
To find a residual, predict with the line, then subtract the prediction from the actual value.
A negative residual means the point is below the line. In the next video, we look at common traps and the fast way with Desmos.
